來源未提供具體作曲家或曲目。Khloy的實際演奏場合主要見於柬埔寨高棉傳統音樂中: The source names no particular composer or piece. The khloy is actually played mainly in informal solos within Khmer traditional music in Cambodia; unlike the Thai klui, the khloy is usually played solo. When listening, note that it mostly uses a pentatonic scale, and distinguish the two sizes, the higher khloy ek and the lower khloy thomm. On some instruments a hole above the highest fingerhole is covered with rice paper or a bamboo membrane, giving a recognisable membrane hole.
克洛伊笛屬氣鳴笛，有大小兩制：khloy ek 音高較高，khloy thomm: The khloy is an aerophone flute in two sizes: the khloy ek is higher and the khloy thomm lower. The holes are either six fingerholes plus a thumb hole, or seven fingerholes with no thumb hole, and it mostly uses a pentatonic scale. It is close to the Thai klui, but the Khmer khloy is older and, unlike the klui, is mostly played solo on informal occasions.
克洛伊笛是柬埔寨高棉人的傳統竹製豎吹氣鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs: The khloy is a traditional bamboo vertical aerophone of the Khmer people of Cambodia, Hornbostel–Sachs number 421.221.12. It comes in two sizes, the higher khloy ek and the lower khloy thomm. The body usually has six fingerholes and a thumb hole, or seven fingerholes and no thumb hole; the hole above the highest fingerhole may be covered with rice paper or a bamboo membrane. It is mostly played solo on informal occasions and commonly uses a pentatonic scale.
克洛伊笛琴身以竹製成，屬竹製氣鳴樂器。來源僅載明最高指孔上方之孔可覆以米紙或竹內: The body of the khloy is bamboo; it is a bamboo aerophone. The source records only that the hole above the highest fingerhole may be covered with rice paper or a membrane made from the inner skin of bamboo; the materials of the mouth hole, the body, the fingerholes and any fittings are not recorded. No reed or other sounding component is mentioned, so only the bamboo tube and the membrane can be confirmed.
克洛伊笛的歷史可從碑文與雕刻追溯。九九四年庫克普拉薩特（Kuk Prasat）寺: The history of the khloy can be traced through inscriptions and carvings. The word kluy already appears on the base of Kuk Prasat temple in 994, later becoming khluy or khloy in modern Khmer; the foundation stele of Preah Ko temple in the ninth century is inscribed with the Sanskrit venu. As for images, a flute is depicted on a lintel of Sambor Prey Kuk temple in the seventh century, and its form also appears in the bas-reliefs of Phnom Bakheng of the late ninth to tenth century. Because bamboo is abundant in Southeast Asia, similar bamboo flutes are distributed across Asia.

The fingers cover six fingerholes and a thumb hole, or follow a layout of seven fingerholes with no thumb hole. If there is another hole above the highest fingerhole, it can be covered with rice paper or a bamboo-skin membrane. A beginner should first learn the fingering of the pentatonic scale, then practise in the manner of an informal solo.
